name: Lamayuru
tagline: Ladakh's old gompa above the eroded moonland
meta_description: Lamayuru, Ladakh: one of the oldest gompas, the eroded moonland, Wanla and Fotu La. Distances from Leh, costs, stays and how to fit it into your trip.
summary: Lamayuru is a Drikung Kagyu monastery and village at about 3,510 m on the Srinagar–Leh highway, 125 km west of Leh. It is one of the oldest and largest gompas in Ladakh, set above pale eroded lake sediments people call moonland. See it as a long day trip or a night on the road to Kargil.
intro: Coming from Leh, the highway leaves the Indus at Khalatse and climbs a narrow gorge. Then the valley opens and Lamayuru appears all at once: white monastery buildings stacked on a crag, mud-brick houses spilling down below it, and around them a strange landscape of soft yellow and grey ridges cut into fins and gullies by wind and water. Most visitors stop for an hour. We think it deserves a night.

Lamayuru Monastery belongs to the Drikung Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism and is counted among the largest and oldest gompas in Ladakh. Tradition says the valley was once a lake, and that the Indian teacher Naropa caused it to drain before a monastery was founded on its shore. Whatever you make of the story, the pale ground around the village does look like old lake bed, and the monastery's oldest shrines sit on the rock above it.

Lamayuru also matters for planning. At 3,510 m it is almost exactly the height of Leh, so on the road from Srinagar it is a good place to sleep after Kargil (2,676 m) before arriving in Leh. Going the other way, it is the start of classic treks into Zanskar and the Sham valley, and the gateway to Fotu La (4,108 m), the highest point on the Srinagar–Leh highway.
facts: 1, or a day trip from Leh
Old Drikung Kagyu gompa, moonland, treks to Zanskar

highlights.title: Lamayuru Monastery at prayer time
highlights.text: Climb into the assembly hall in the early morning when monks gather for prayers with horns, cymbals and butter tea. Look for the small cave shrine linked by tradition to Naropa. Visitors sit quietly at the back; ask before any photography.

highlights.title: The moonland ridges
highlights.text: Below the village, soft pale sediments have weathered into fins, towers and gullies. They glow yellow at sunset and turn grey at noon. The best views are from the highway bends just east of the village and from the monastery roof.

highlights.title: Wanla's small hilltop temple
highlights.text: About 10 km south on a side road, Wanla village has a small, old temple to Avalokiteshvara on a ridge with a ruined fort. It sees few visitors. Ask in the village for the caretaker with the key.

highlights.title: Fotu La on the road to Kargil
highlights.text: Fifteen kilometres west, the highway crosses Fotu La at 4,108 m, the highest pass on the Srinagar–Leh road. The top has prayer flags and long views back over Lamayuru. Stop briefly; do not linger if you have just arrived.

highlights.title: Trailhead for Zanskar and Sham treks
highlights.text: Lamayuru is the classic start of the long trek south to Padum in Zanskar and of shorter routes over the passes to Wanla, Hinju and Chilling. Arrange ponies and a guide in Leh, not on arrival.

highlights.title: Khalatse and its apricots
highlights.text: On the way from Leh, Khalatse sits low on the Indus at about 3,000 m, with two crops a year and orchards along the road. Stop for apricot juice in July or dried fruit the rest of the year.

field_notes.fact: Tradition holds that the Lamayuru valley was once filled by a lake, and that the Buddhist teacher Naropa caused the water to drain away before the monastery was founded. A small cave in the monastery is linked to his meditation.
Lamayuru is one of the largest and oldest gompas in Ladakh and belongs to the Drikung Kagyu school, the same lineage that runs Phyang Monastery near Leh.
Fotu La, about 15 km west of Lamayuru, is at 4,108 m the highest point on the Srinagar–Leh highway, higher than Zoji La and Namika La.

local_word.meaning: a solitary or remote place; the everyday word for a monastery

costs: Guesthouse room with dinner and breakfast
Thukpa or a plate of rice, dal and vegetables

how_to_reach.text: Fly to Leh and rest two nights there first. Lamayuru is a long day out from Leh or a stop on the road to Kargil.

Buses from Leh to Kargil pass through Lamayuru, usually leaving Leh early in the morning; the fare is roughly ₹250–400. Coming back, flag down the Kargil–Leh bus on the highway. Timings change by season, so check current status before you travel.
From Leh ≈ 125 km · 3.5–4 h on the Srinagar highway via Nimmu, Saspol and Khalatse. From Kargil ≈ 105 km · 3 h via Mulbekh, Namika La and Fotu La. Combine with Alchi and Likir on the way.

where_to_stay: Saver: a handful of family guesthouses and small hotels line the highway and the lane below the monastery, with simple rooms at ₹1,500–3,000 per person including dinner and breakfast; some have shared bathrooms. Comfort: the best rooms here are still plain, so comfort travellers often sleep at Alchi or the Sham valley and visit Lamayuru by car. Signature: there is no luxury hotel; we base you at Nimmu House and plan Lamayuru as an unhurried day out.
tips: Reach the monastery by 7 am for prayers, or after 4 pm when the day-trip cars have gone.
Lamayuru sits at Leh's height, so it is a sensible night on the road from Srinagar and Kargil before Leh.
Carry cash from Leh or Kargil; there is no reliable ATM in the village.
Do not climb the soft moonland ridges; they crumble easily and the scars stay for years.
If you are starting a trek here, spend at least three nights in Leh first and arrange ponies in advance.

experiences.title: Morning prayers at Lamayuru Monastery
experiences.summary: Sleep in the village and walk up before the day-trip cars arrive, to sit at the back of the assembly hall while the monks of this Drikung Kagyu gompa chant, drink butter tea and sound the long horns.
body: Lamayuru's assembly hall comes to life early. The monks file in, take their places on long cushions, and begin the morning recitation. A young monk moves along the rows pouring butter tea, and at intervals the chanting gives way to drums, cymbals and the low note of the long horns. Visitors are welcome to sit quietly at the back.

After prayers, walk around the hall and look for the small cave shrine that tradition links to Naropa, the teacher who is said to have drained the lake that once filled this valley. Then climb to the roof. In the low morning light the moonland ridges below the village look like a model of a mountain range, and you can trace the highway winding towards Fotu La.

Arrive by 6.30 am. Dress modestly, remove shoes and hats where asked, keep your phone silent and do not walk in front of monks during prayers. Photography inside is often not allowed; ask first and accept the answer.

faqs.q: What time are morning prayers at Lamayuru?
faqs.a: Morning prayers usually start between 6 and 7 am, a little later in cold months. Times change with the season and the monastery calendar, so ask your guesthouse the evening before. Arrive a few minutes early, sit at the back, and stay until the end of a section rather than walking out mid-chant.

faqs.q: Can I take photographs inside Lamayuru Monastery?
faqs.a: Rules vary by room. Photography is usually restricted inside shrines and during prayers, and flash is never acceptable. Ask a monk or the ticket office before you raise a camera. Exteriors, the roof view and the moonland are fine to photograph, but ask before photographing individual monks.

faqs.q: Is Lamayuru worth an overnight stay?
faqs.a: Yes, if you can spare it. Day-trippers from Leh arrive around midday, when the light is flat and the halls are busy. Staying the night lets you see morning prayers, sunset on the moonland and a quiet village. It also breaks the long drive between Leh and Kargil at a sensible altitude.

experiences.title: Sunset walk along Lamayuru's moonland
experiences.summary: An easy evening walk from the village along the lanes and the old highway, looking over the eroded lake sediments that give Lamayuru its moonland nickname, while the light turns the ridges yellow and gold.
body: The pale, soft ridges around Lamayuru are made of fine sediment laid down when water stood in this valley. Wind and rare rain have cut them into fins and towers. They are not rock you can scramble on, and that is the point of this walk: you look, from paths and roads, rather than climb.

Start at the monastery gate around 5 pm and walk down through the village lanes, past chortens and mani walls, to the old road below. Follow it east for a kilometre to the bends where the highway loops above the moonland. The view back takes in the gompa on its crag with the ridges below. Return the same way as the light fades.
Wear proper shoes, carry a warm layer and a torch, and walk slowly; you are at Leh's height. Stay on paths and road edges, keep away from crumbling drops, and watch for trucks on the highway bends.

faqs.a: The name comes from the pale, eroded sediments around the village, which have weathered into ridges and gullies that look unlike the bare rock elsewhere in Ladakh. Tradition says a lake once filled the valley. The name is a nickname used by drivers and travellers, not a formal place name.

No. It follows village lanes and the road with gentle gradients, about 3–4 km in total. The main challenge is altitude: Lamayuru is about 3,510 m, so walk slowly if you have recently arrived. Avoid climbing onto the soft ridges, which crumble underfoot.

faqs.q: When is the best light at Lamayuru?
faqs.a: The hour before sunset gives warm side light on the ridges and the monastery, from about 5.30 pm in summer. Early morning is also good and quieter. Midday light is flat and harsh, which is when most day-trippers arrive.

experiences.title: Wanla village and its hilltop temple
experiences.summary: A short drive south of Lamayuru, Wanla is a farming village with an old Avalokiteshvara temple and ruined fort on a ridge. Few travellers stop, so the lanes, fields and temple are quiet.
body: From Lamayuru, a side road drops south through a gorge to Wanla, about 10 km away, where the valley widens into barley fields and willow groves along the stream. Above the village, a small temple dedicated to Avalokiteshvara stands with the ruins of an old fort on a narrow ridge.

Ask in the village for the caretaker who keeps the temple key; someone will usually walk up with you. Inside, a large image of Avalokiteshvara rises through the building, and old paintings cover the walls. Leave a small donation. Then walk back through the fields, where in July and August families are irrigating and weeding by hand.

Wanla is also on the trekking route from Lamayuru over Prinkiti La, so you may meet trekkers and pony teams. The road continues to Hinju and towards Konze La. Carry water and snacks; Wanla has only a small shop.

faqs.q: How do I get from Lamayuru to Wanla?
faqs.a: Wanla is about 10 km from Lamayuru by a side road off the highway. A taxi from Lamayuru costs roughly ₹1,500–2,000 return with waiting time. Fit trekkers can also walk there over Prinkiti La in 3–4 hours with a local guide.

faqs.q: Is the Wanla temple always open?
faqs.a: Not always. The temple is kept locked and a caretaker from the village opens it for visitors. Ask in the village; you may have to wait a little. Leave a donation of ₹50–100 and remove your shoes inside.

Yes, a few families in Wanla offer simple homestay rooms, mainly used by trekkers, with dinner and breakfast at about ₹1,500–2,000 per person. Bathrooms are often shared and basic. Most travellers visit as a half-day trip from Lamayuru instead.

faqs.q: How far is Lamayuru from Leh?
faqs.a: Lamayuru is about 125 km west of Leh on the Srinagar highway, a drive of 3.5–4 hours via Nimmu, Saspol and Khalatse. A union taxi day trip costs roughly ₹7,000–9,000 for the car. Many people combine it with Alchi and Likir, or stop here on the way to Kargil.

Yes, especially if you are driving between Leh and Kargil. The monastery is one of the oldest and largest in Ladakh, and the eroded moonland around it looks unlike anywhere else on the highway. If you only have a week flying in and out of Leh, Nubra and Pangong may come first.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Lamayuru?
faqs.a: No. Lamayuru is on the Srinagar–Leh highway and does not need an Inner Line Permit, Protected Area Permit or the environment fee receipt used for Nubra and Pangong. Carry photo ID for routine checks. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Lamayuru and will I get altitude sickness?
faqs.a: Lamayuru is about 3,510 m, close to Leh's height. If you have already spent two nights in Leh it should feel similar. If you are coming from Srinagar, sleeping at Kargil (2,676 m) first and then Lamayuru is a gentle way up. Talk to your doctor before travel if you have heart or lung conditions.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in Lamayuru?
faqs.a: Yes. Several family guesthouses and small hotels near the monastery and on the highway charge about ₹1,500–3,000 per person with dinner and breakfast. Rooms are simple and some have shared bathrooms. Book ahead in July and August when trekking groups pass through.

Lamayuru holds masked-dance festivals on dates set by the Tibetan lunar calendar; the best known is Yuru Kabgyat, which usually falls in summer. Dates move each year, so check current status with the monastery or a Leh travel agency before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network and an ATM in Lamayuru?
faqs.a: Coverage is patchy: BSNL and some postpaid networks work near the highway, but do not rely on data. Prepaid SIMs from outside Ladakh do not work. There is no reliable ATM, so carry enough cash from Leh or Kargil for rooms, food and monastery fees.

Yes. Lamayuru is the start of the long trek south to Padum in Zanskar, usually 10 days or more, and of shorter routes to Wanla, Hinju and over Konze La to Chilling. Arrange a guide and ponies through a registered Leh agency, and acclimatise in Leh for at least three nights first.

faqs.q: Is Lamayuru suitable for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes, as a day trip or one night. The monastery visit involves stairs and uneven floors but no long walk, and children usually enjoy the moonland views. The drive from Leh is long, so plan stops at Alchi or Khalatse. Carry warm layers, snacks and water.
